Question: What can a two-hour test check before a tenant starts a 30–90 day training run?
- IDENTIFIER through IDENTIFIER: accepted child result records.
- IDENTIFIER: ten source notes with access limits and proposed checks.
- IDENTIFIER through IDENTIFIER: supplement review records.
Keep all writes inside this research run directory.
Do not use the two-hour test in place of GPU, network, storage, internet, inference, or lifecycle category tests.
It makes changes to selected platform reading only. It does not make changes to operational recovery sources.

MegaScale’s production workflow sends heartbeats with executor/process status, logs and RDMA metrics. It checks for missed heartbeats/anomalous traffic. It puts a stop to the job, runs diagnostics, and removes faulty nodes. It then starts again from a checkpoint.

Its two-stage checkpoint puts GPU state into host memory first. Training runs again from that copy. The system then sends the checkpoint to HDFS asynchronously. On restart, one worker uses the shared partitions. The worker sends them to all ranks.

Varuna uses pipeline and data parallelism together. Spot resources make changes over time. Varuna makes dynamic changes to pipeline depth/data replicas in response. It makes periodic checkpoints at mini-batch boundaries.
It makes a checkpoint of each layer independently. It puts the writes in shards across data-parallel replicas. It puts writes on local SSD first. In the background, it sends copies to cloud storage.

Loss spikes do not necessarily show hardware faults. Optimization dynamics, data outliers, numerical precision, and infrastructure can all make contributions. Triage must use loss plus gradient norm, scaler/overflow and skipped-step counters, sample/data position, per-rank consistency, GPU/NVLink/network telemetry, and logs.
For Closed division, MLPerf Training checks wall-clock time. The check uses a complete benchmark run to its defined quality target. The check runs under benchmark-specific rules.

Two hours can show measured behavior under this configuration. It cannot show behavior under different tenant recipes or later software changes. [inference] MegaScale’s findings keep a close tie to full-stack, per-rank observability at scale. [observed] SOURCE

6. **Restart semantic correctness:** Make a controlled interruption after committed step k. Put back the model, optimizer, scheduler, scaler, data cursor/shard position, and RNG states. Check the next-step inputs and state continuity. Check the resumed trajectory against uninterrupted control. Use tolerances appropriate to nondeterministic distributed math. Check loss/gradients and step counters, not only the job restart. [inference] SOURCE

7. **Fault response:** Put at least one process failure into the run. Put a node/link fault where safe. Check detection, restart/replacement time, lost work since the durable checkpoint, and the return to useful throughput. One successful injected event makes a narrow proof. It shows only that event/path, and only once. [inference] SOURCE · SOURCE

A GPU-to-host-memory snapshot makes the staging step. Async file/object writes make the persistence step. Atomic publication makes a separate protocol step. A valid generation must show a consistent optimizer step across shards and metadata.

- **Checkpoint approach does not make one category:** CheckFreq runs a pipeline of snapshot and durable persistence. It keeps the iterator position. MegaScale puts GPU state in host memory, then sends it to HDFS asynchronously. Oobleck puts missing state back via pipeline replicas. Varuna uses elastic morphing with periodic layer-wise checkpointing to local SSD and background cloud copy. The sources show different mechanisms and failure assumptions. [observed] Sources: SOURCE, SOURCE, SOURCE, SOURCE

- **Keep failure rates separate:** Meta’s two-cluster trace study shows job failure exposure variation by job scale and failure causes. Its fleet-scale observations make useful evidence. They show long-run exposure to diverse events. But they do not make a rate for this Chennai rack. [observed/inference] SOURCE

Layered evidence makes the strongest bridge to a 30–90-day commitment. Use these layers: two-hour measured acceptance + explicit restart test + continued production telemetry, checkpoint-retention/restore drills, alerting and operational SLA

- **Moderate:** The gradient-noise-scale primary study shows support for the limited interpretation of the statistic. The application to arbitrary Llama-class recipes keeps a workload-dependent character.
- The briefs show no exact tenant model, token budget, optimizer, data pipeline, checkpoint destination, or acceptance thresholds. The tenant must make these choices for workload-faithful tests.
- No public study shows a defensible conversion. The target conversion: this particular 18-tray GB300-class, Chennai rack’s two-hour exposure to a 54-day run-success probability.

This research checks public AI-lab training records for operational health and scientifically valid recovery. Rack-bench does not use vendor specifications as PASS evidence. Rack-bench runs measured category checks (~2h/category) on an 18-tray GB300-class NVL72 rack. A training microbenchmark can show a specified workload that runs reproducibly. It can show measured throughput, MFU, loss behavior, and checkpoint/resume correctness in the tested software/configuration. It cannot show multi-week failure rate, day/night stability, the tail of recovery times, or correctness across all interruption causes. **[inference]**
The scale and duration of the Llama 3, OPT, and BLOOM records make that separation directly. The records show many weeks and real interruptions, not a short acceptance run.

3. **MFU makes an accounting convention, not a self-validating scalar.** The numerator uses model FLOPs/token and useful token throughput. The denominator uses accelerator count, precision-specific theoretical peak, and time window. Dense-vs-MoE, recomputation, padded/dropped tokens, warmup, and evaluation/checkpoint pauses can make a material difference to the interpretation. Also check the QUOTE label: a precision-appropriate Tensor Core peak, or another definition. [inference] SOURCE; SOURCE; SOURCE.
The paper’s table puts QUOTE on its percentage column. The listed subtype percentages do not all show agreement with the stated unexpected-event denominator.

For HBM3, the table puts 72 events; 72 / 466 = 15.5%, and 72 / 419 = 17.2%. The table’s HBM3 percentage shows agreement with the latter. **Do not use the subtype table percentages as a set with one consistently auditable denominator.** Use the paper’s prose-level 58.7% as the anchor for citations. Use subtype counts in place of copied percentages; the counts make safer evidence. [calculated] (SOURCE)

- The paper shows these GPU-related subtype counts. The counts show 148 faulty-GPU events, 72 GPU HBM3 memory events, and 19 GPU SRAM memory events. The counts also show 17 GPU system-processor events, 6 silent-data-corruption events, and 6 thermal-interface/sensor events. The paper also shows 35 switch/cable network events and 54 software-bug events.
The paper shows other host/dependency categories too. The source does not show the full taxonomy details. Do not make blind sums of the counts into mutually exclusive root causes. [observed] (SOURCE)

In synchronous training, one GPU failure can start a whole distributed job restart. Meta shows these measures: production-grade automated maintenance, reduced startup/checkpoint time, and rapid diagnosis tooling. Meta also shows PyTorch NCCL flight-recorder metadata and stack traces. Watchdog/heartbeat timeout starts automatic trace dumps. Meta starts extra tracing online without a job restart. NVLink failures can show stalled GPU load/store operations without clean error codes.

The update also shows a dataset formatting problem. The problem makes implausibly low perplexity (JSON escaping/whitespace/corpus formatting). The update also shows a warning. Operators must check loss metrics with data-pipeline sanity checks. These records make dated author reports, not a normalized event-rate dataset.

The BLOOM logbook also shows an LM-loss spike. The spike makes a sharp rise for a few steps. It runs back near baseline in ~30 iterations. The logbook shows a concurrent gradient-norm spike. The logbook does not automatically put a fatal-divergence label on it. Elsewhere the logbook shows evaluation deadlocks.

- Show the MFU basis: only analytically necessary model FLOPs, or all executed work. Activation recomputation makes the executed operation count larger. The model-FLOPs MFU convention keeps recomputation overhead separate from hardware FLOPs utilization (HFU). Both can make useful measures. But the measures put different questions. [inference] (SOURCE; SOURCE)

One benchmark setup keeps warmup out of steady-state MFU. It keeps warmup wall time inside end-to-end goodput. That benchmark can show MFU efficiency. It can still make fewer useful tokens per wall-clock hour.

BLOOM runs a multi-dataset evaluation once every 1,000 iterations. The observed cost runs at ~7 training iterations (~0.7%). Llama 3 checks adaptation after context-length changes with short-context eval recovery and needle-in-a-haystack tests. DeepSeek’s public report shows no irrecoverable spikes/rollbacks. It does not show a universal evaluation cadence (SOURCE; SOURCE; SOURCE). These records show one lesson: eval makes both a measurable throughput cost and an essential model-quality signal. [observed]
4. RNG states for Python, NumPy, framework CPU, and each GPU/rank; check RNG synchronization where the setup uses topology/parallel ranks.

This inventory makes a correctness requirement. The inference uses optimizer dynamics. The public logs directly make the motivation: optimizer-state, TP-rank, and RNG synchronization problems. This text does not make a blanket claim. The cited labs do not all publicly show every field (SOURCE; SOURCE).

Check that the restart does not repeat data silently. Check that it does not skip data silently. Do not put a partially written checkpoint in use as complete. A process at QUOTE does not show equivalence by itself.

This list makes proposed actionable two-hour checks. Public mechanisms and incidents make the basis (SOURCE; SOURCE; SOURCE). No claim here shows these exact tests as published universal industry protocol.
- equivalence to a customer’s exact model, data, precision, training framework, or distributed parallelism, in cases with differences from the rack-bench workload;

- **High confidence:** the primary Meta paper shows interruption totals, scope, definitions, tooling, and the MFU table. DeepSeek’s own technical report shows its reported stability/recipe. First-party BLOOM operational chronicles show timestamps, checkpoint policy, and concrete state bugs. Each source keeps a team attribution. But the reports keep self-reported status. The BLOOM logbook makes a dated public operational diary, not a controlled reliability study.

- **Medium confidence:** arithmetic from those records keeps a transparent basis. But it also keeps source taxonomy and denominator limitations. Llama Table 5 shows percentage denominator inconsistencies. So prose claims and raw counts make safer evidence than subtype percentages.

- **Not established:** independent reproduction of Llama/DeepSeek production telemetry, all event-level root-cause records, event-by-event MTTR. Also not established: a public 30–90-day trial of the target rack class.

- Kept: SOURCE. Primary dated author update, fetched for specific numerical-instability, data-formatting and restart incidents; not a full logbook/event census. Gemini shows a separately labeled secondary summary of failure counts and wasted GPU-hours.
- Dropped: general commercial training/recovery blogs and non-primary MFU explainers. This research removes them where primary reports or the systems paper show the claim.

- Llama Table 5’s printed subtype percentages do not consistently show agreement with raw counts under one denominator. The prose denominator for 78% and 58.7% keeps clarity: 419 unexpected events. This research does not make up a reconciliation for every table percentage.

This report uses three claim marks: [observed] (explicitly present in source), [calculated] (arithmetic), [inference] (application to rack certification). This research node runs independently. Scope: a GB300-class NVL72-class rack (18 trays) in Chennai. Category checks use measured data, about two hours per category, plus smoke burn-in. PASS shows a measured result, not a vendor claim.

[Observed] PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint (DCP) documentation shows multi-rank parallel save/load. It shows load-time resharding across cluster topologies. DCP makes multiple files and runs in place. It does not currently make backwards-compatibility guarantees for saved state dictionaries. The current stable page shows PyTorch 2.14.0 and last update July 8, 2026. SOURCE

[Inference] These records show general reliability context; they do not show operational distributed-training validation. Keep the book beside DMLS. Do not put it above current recovery guides. The SOURCE keeps metadata conflicts and full-text limits.
They show direct platform context for training metrics, data management, and artifact records.

[Observed] NVIDIA makes DCGM diagnostics for GPU deployment/readiness, active hardware/integration/stress tests, and health telemetry. The diagnostics run in an invasive way. They can use GPU, memory, PCIe, NVLink, CPU, power, and cooling resources. Check with the scheduler. Keep the tested resources isolated. SOURCE

The public evidence does not show a 54-day run or model convergence from a two-hour test. It does not even show restart correctness end to end. The article shows no procedure or acceptance criterion for Llama loss-trend triage. It shows no criterion for checkpoint-resume numerical equivalence, interruption accounting/goodput during actual training, or multi-day stability. SemiAnalysis explicitly shows this limit: its hands-on process cannot directly check reliability over time or performance at scale. [observed] SOURCE

For its sample, SemiAnalysis makes one request. The request: 32 GPUs (four 8-GPU HGX nodes or eight 4-GPU NVL72 nodes). The request also puts high-bandwidth networking, file and object storage, and dashboards on the list. The request runs up to five days each for Slurm and Kubernetes testing.

The target rack here makes a material difference in topology and context. Its context: 18 GB300-class trays in one NVL72-class rack, Chennai. ClusterMAX shows tests across heterogeneous allocations/providers. ClusterMAX shows no complete same-rack test recipe or results for this exact Chennai configuration. Therefore, keep the direct application of its findings to this target limited.

The public IDENTIFIER CLI explicitly makes an audit tool. It makes only an initial subset of the full internal suite. It checks installed versions, hardware/software inventory, scheduler and container setup, networking configuration, health telemetry, and selected binary checks. The README shows one omission. The omitted criteria make performance, reliability, provider-side, commercial/contractual, or scale-out evidence necessary. Core audit does not run planned performance or reliability tests. [observed] SOURCE

Accordingly, IDENTIFIER can make a useful preflight on prerequisites (for example GPU/device visibility, topology/NCCL configuration, utilities, and health instrumentation). But IDENTIFIER alone does not make certifications for achieved Llama throughput, MFU, convergence, recovery correctness, or long-run reliability. The repo also shows an exclusion list: benchmark implementations, provider results, internal notes, private dashboard, and database code.

The 3.0 methodology shows per-GPU GEMM and grouped-GEMM measurements across supported precisions and model-like shapes. It also shows memory bandwidth/copy tests and HPL-MxP. HPL-MxP uses compute, memory, MPI, NVLink, and numerical correctness together. But it makes a linear-system benchmark, not evidence of optimizer convergence or correct model training. [observed] SOURCE

Their results can show configuration and fabric bottlenecks relevant to training. But benchmark output does not itself make a full training goodput or 54-day reliability measurement. [observed methodology; inference on implication] SOURCE

The article shows no fixed run duration, token/step count, or seed for these two training jobs. It shows no target loss curve, convergence threshold, repeatability tolerance, or per-provider MFU results. It makes no statement that training passes use converged loss. It also shows no standardized loss-triage rubric. Therefore, the article shows coverage of a runnable short training workload. It does not show a public reproducible convergence acceptance protocol. [observed, bounded to published methodology] SOURCE

The published burn-in runs eight hours: large tensor-core GEMMs and all-to-all communications run simultaneously. Monitoring keeps records of temperature, power, clock, FLOPs, connectivity, latency, bandwidth, and kernel-ring-buffer errors. This can show concurrent-load, thermal, clock-throttling, and hard-error symptoms during that interval. It makes a materially stronger test than a two-hour-only stress test. But it does not show multi-day reliability. [observed] SOURCE

The fault handling tests run separately. The tests use node reboots. They put in DCGM errors or synthetic XID/SXID kernel messages. The final method uses a PCIe bridge reset to make a genuine XID 79. Then the tests check the timing of detection, drain, and return-to-command availability. This checks provider health-check and scheduler/remediation behavior.

Crucially, this framing makes upcoming evaluation of RL/post-training infrastructure. It does not make evidence that ClusterMAX 3.0's Llama 3.1 pretraining suite already uses those measures. [observed] SOURCE

The sibling storage brief shows the DCP checkpoint save/load and Skild AI datagen methodology at IDENTIFIER, lines 21–22 (§1.2). This makes inherited secondary research, not independently verified benchmark execution or locally reproduced results. The primary methodology article itself shows both tests. SOURCE [local source: IDENTIFIER]
The following make QUOTE not claims that SemiAnalysis never runs them privately or that no provider does them.

A two-hour category check cannot run ClusterMAX's eight-hour burn-in. It cannot run the longer provider evaluation. It can still make useful, measured evidence. But make its short-window-screen role explicit.

Check (d): loss/gradient/parameter finite values and trend review against the run's expected short-horizon behavior. Check (e): GPU clocks/temperature/power/ECC/XID and NCCL errors correlated to steps. Run (f): one checkpoint save and restore, then a deterministic or tolerance-bounded state/output comparison under an explicitly controlled recipe. These items make proposed rack-bench checks, not procedures from ClusterMAX.

- **High confidence about public CLI limits:** The README explicitly shows the CLI as an audit. The README shows an omission of performance/reliability tests and provider results/benchmark implementations. [observed] SOURCE

- SemiAnalysis’ internal training scripts, run lengths, exact pass thresholds, loss records, and per-provider results make no public appearance. The inspected corpus shows none of them. Send a direct request for these when they make a difference to the decision.

- The task makes reference to sibling checkpoint/datagen work. This worktree shows none of its implementation artifacts. This brief keeps a link to the sibling storage brief. This brief makes no re-derivation of its storage claims.
The window uses setup, tests, and reporting time.
Keep existing category tests separate.
It does not make GPU, fabric, storage, internet, inference, or lifecycle tests unnecessary.

10. **Verdict report.** Put per-assertion states, raw evidence paths, every attempt, and untested limits in the report.
- GPU, fabric, storage, internet, inference, and lifecycle tests run separately
- Does it use a checkpoint, or does it run the job from the beginning?
- Which auto-resume settings does it use?
- How much space does one checkpoint use?
- What notice does a preemption send?

The tenant must still keep a recovery design and capacity/lease terms. SOURCE; SOURCE; SOURCE.

[Observed] The AWS documentation shows NVIDIA SMI checks for GPU health and EFA connectivity tests with all available EFA cards. The specific recovery path keeps a conditional status. Slurm GRES allocations can make in-place allocation changes impossible. HyperPod can then put the faulty job back in the queue and start the job again from the beginning. A job with a supported auto-resume arrangement does not run this path.

[Observed] The Azure public CycleCloud Slurm project shows a Healthagent daemon and Slurm IDENTIFIER. These components can put nodes in drain state on health errors. The project configuration runs checks on a 60-second interval, across node states by default in that project documentation. Monitoring can show Node Exporter, NVIDIA DCGM exporter, and AzSlurm scheduler metrics. The AzSlurm exporter shows job terminal states/reasons, node states, provisioning/quota availability, and scheduler-cycle metrics. SOURCE.

[Observed] Microsoft’s CycleCloud Slurm reference shows IDENTIFIER with a default of 1800 seconds. It shows IDENTIFIER placement behavior for tightly coupled MPI nodes. These examples show node startup and placement as configured operational parameters, not instantaneous guarantees. SOURCE.

[Inference] The tenant keeps the exact Azure Slurm/CycleCloud project version and configuration on record, and sends the provider these questions. Which checks put nodes in drain state? Do the checks use intrusive methods? How often do the checks run? Can the tenant check health events? Which topology does the project keep static, and which topology does autoscaling make?

[Observed] Google’s Cloud TPU maintenance guide shows checkpoints approximately hourly as a rule of thumb. Save time can run from seconds to minutes. TPU jobs can make an automatic recovery from most maintenance events. Edge cases can make deletion/recreation of TPU resources and a restart from a saved checkpoint necessary. The guide shows two recommendations: training-script retries only together with checkpoints, and records of maintenance events. SOURCE (page updated 2026-10-09).

[Inference] The provider must send written answers to four questions. Does the provider keep a replacement-hardware guarantee for the entire tenant term? Does replacement keep rack/switch/NVLink/fabric topology intact? Does replacement capacity keep the same SKU and software baseline? Does repair/replacement use up paid lease time?
Two-hour rack tests can show current rank mapping and gross topology/configuration issues. They cannot show future replacement availability or stable placement. SOURCE; SOURCE; SOURCE.

[Inference] The tenant sends questions about event semantics: planned maintenance versus emergency fault. The tenant sends questions about the notice channel, the minimum notice, and the allowed actions. Does the notice make it to the job? Can the tenant make a complete checkpoint within that window?

[Observed] AWS shows GPU and EFA checkers. Azure’s project shows health agents that can put labels or drain states on nodes. The operational pattern shows error detection and unhealthy-node exclusion before or during scheduling. The pattern makes no promise of zero new faults. SOURCE; SOURCE.

[Inference] Bench candidate: after the existing burn-in, the bench keeps records of per-GPU error/health telemetry and ECC/XID counters. The bench also keeps records of link state, fabric errors, PCIe/NVLink status, temperatures/power/throttling, kernel logs, and scheduler-visible health state. The bench checks the exclusion of a suspect node from allocation.

[Inference] Run a representative distributed training script at full rack scale. Keep records of rank/world-size, global batch, data-parallel/tensor/pipeline layout, and collective completion. Keep records of loss, tokens/second, and per-rank progress. Check loss for finite values, and check that loss runs within the expected tolerance. Where feasible, check the results against a known-good reference/configuration.

Run an all-reduce/checksum or a deterministic small validation batch before/after checkpoint restore. Success shows valid progress by the workload and participation from all ranks. Success does not show convergence of a 54-day optimization to a target model quality. SOURCE; SOURCE; SOURCE.

If supported, run an interrupted or partial-write scenario safely. Remove incomplete checkpoints from the selection. Check checkpoint wall time and restore wall time. Check the data-loss window: steps since the last committed checkpoint. Check the end-to-end time to useful training throughput after the restart. SOURCE; SOURCE; SOURCE.

[Observed] Google shows checkpoint times from seconds to minutes. Google shows recovery from the saved checkpoint. AWS auto-resume likewise makes a restart from the last saved checkpoint. Its GRES caveat can make a restart from the beginning necessary. SOURCE; SOURCE.

Keep records of step-time distributions, per-rank skew, and GPU utilization. Keep records of network utilization/retries, storage throughput/latency, and CPU utilization. Keep records of dataloader wait time, queue depth, and input-cache behavior.
Use representative dataset reads and enough warm/cold data to make obvious stalls visible. Keep metric records at a cadence that shows stall/step-time-spike correlation. SOURCE; SOURCE; SOURCE.
Check checkpoint duration, restore time, lost steps, and time back to steady useful progress.

1. **Duration and interruption:** What guaranteed start/end time does the lease show? What does lease expiry put an end to? Can the tenant make a lease extension? What result does the boundary make for a running job? AWS Capacity Blocks show the importance of exact end-of-block semantics. SOURCE.

2. **Notice and action:** Which event types send a notice? Which channel does the notice use? What minimum notice does the provider send? Can tenant code make a checkpoint/exit before termination? Google shows GPU notices by family, not a universal GPU rule. SOURCE.

3. **Replacement:** Does the provider keep capacity in reserve for replacement nodes for the full term? Can a replacement make changes to tray/rack/fabric topology, GPU count, software baseline, or rank mapping? Does the contract make replacement downtime billable? SOURCE.

4. **Recovery semantics:** Does recovery make a node reboot/replacement, a job restart, or only a requeue? Does the job make a resume from the latest committed checkpoint or the beginning? Which scheduler/GRES/launcher configurations can the job use? SOURCE.

5. **Checkpoint:** Which state does the checkpoint keep, and what storage does it use? How often does the job make a checkpoint commit? What durability/retention does the contract put in place? What restore time does the demonstration show? Google shows roughly hourly checkpoints as a starting point, not a service-level promise. SOURCE.

6. **Observability and escalation:** Can the tenant check job, GPU, fabric, storage, dataloader, health-agent, and maintenance events with timestamps? Who puts nodes in drain state or makes node repairs? What response-time commitment does the provider show? Azure’s published monitoring examples show useful metrics, but they do not make an SLA for this rack. SOURCE.

3. [Observed] Google shows a recommendation for frequent checkpoints. Google shows GPU maintenance notice and stop behavior with variation by GPU family. TPU recovery can still make resource recreation and restart necessary. SOURCE; SOURCE.
4. [Observed] Lease/capacity end semantics can put an end to active jobs. The tenant must check exact reservation duration and replacement capacity independently of rack health. SOURCE; SOURCE.

5. [Inference] Keep PASS scoped to the measured rack/workload/configuration. Show the specific tested checkpoint/restart result in the PASS disclosure. Never make hyperscaler documentation or a two-hour PASS into an unsupported GB300 reliability claim.

The page separately shows a P5.4xlarge EFA/NCCL GPU-to-GPU compatibility issue. The mitigation uses EFA 1.43.1+ and IDENTIFIER. Do not put that P5.4xlarge-specific workaround on P5.48xlarge, P5e, or another platform automatically. Check the live SKU table and release notes before freeze. SOURCE.

[Proposal] On the tested rack, keep records of IDENTIFIER output and driver/CUDA/runtime/framework/NCCL versions. Put IDENTIFIER in the version records. Keep records of IDENTIFIER or the actual fabric’s equivalent inventory, loaded NIC/RDMA libraries, and container-visible device mappings.

[Proposal] For an ND-inspired preflight, keep records of actual node/SKU, GPU count, and driver/CUDA/NCCL/MPI/PMIx versions. Keep records of IDENTIFIER, GPU↔NIC/RDMA device association, and link state/rate. Keep records of Slurm node/GRES, rank mapping, topology file/plugin, and placement boundaries.

Run the same NCCL collective across one node and all allocated nodes. Keep a record of the selected path against the expected InfiniBand/GPU-direct path. Also keep records of correctness/error count, bus bandwidth, and per-rank skew.
The guide shows an IDENTIFIER build/run under Slurm, eight GPUs per node. It checks collective output including IDENTIFIER and out-of-bounds counts. SOURCE.

Then run NCCL tests at intra-node and full-rack scope with the production launcher/container. Check collective correctness (IDENTIFIER/out-of-bounds zero). Check the expected network plugin/path, no timeout, and stable per-rank participation.

- **Identity and versions:** rack/tray inventory; GPU model/count; OS/kernel; BIOS/BMC/firmware; driver; CUDA; NCCL. Also: framework and PyTorch-bundled NCCL; MPI/PMIx; scheduler; container digest; fabric plugin/driver. Keep exact output and timestamp records. SOURCE; SOURCE.
